> ## Theme Using your theme variables
> Theme | tailwindcss@4.x | Source: https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss.com/blob/main/src/docs/theme.mdx
>
> ## Using your theme variables
>
> All of your theme variables are turned into regular CSS variables when you compile your CSS:
>
> ```css
> /* [!code filename:dist.css] */
> :root {
>   /* prettier-ignore */
>   --font-sans: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", "Noto Sans", Arial, sans-serif, "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji", "Segoe UI Symbol", "Noto Color Emoji";
>   --font-serif: ui-serif, Georgia, Cambria, "Times New Roman", Times, serif;
>   --font-mono: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", "Courier New", monospace;
>
>   --color-red-50: oklch(0.971 0.013 17.38);
>   --color-red-100: oklch(0.936 0.032 17.717);
>   --color-red-200: oklch(0.885 0.062 18.334);
>   /* ... */
>
>   --shadow-2xs: 0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05);
>   --shadow-xs: 0 1px 2px 0 rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05);
>   --shadow-sm: 0 1px 3px 0 rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1), 0 1px 2px -1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1);
>   /* ... */
> }
> ```
>
> This makes it easy to reference all of your design tokens in any of your custom CSS or inline styles.
>
> ### With custom CSS
>
> Use your theme variables to get access to your design tokens when you're writing custom CSS that needs to use the same values:
>
> ```css
> /* [!code filename:app.css] */
> /* [!code word:var(--text-base)] */
> /* [!code word:var(--color-gray-700)] */
> /* [!code word:var(--text-2xl)] */
> /* [!code word:var(--font-weight-semibold)] */
> /* [!code word:var(--color-gray-950)] */
> /* [!code word:var(--text-xl)] */
> @import "tailwindcss";
>
> @layer components {
>   .typography {
>     p {
>       font-size: var(--text-base);
>       color: var(--color-gray-700);
>     }
>
>     h1 {
>       font-size: var(--text-2xl--line-height);
>       font-weight: var(--font-weight-semibold);
>       color: var(--color-gray-950);
>     }
>
>     h2 {
>       font-size: var(--text-xl);
>       font-weight: var(--font-weight-semibold);
>       color: var(--color-gray-950);
>     }
>   }
> }
> ```
>
> This is often useful when styling HTML you don't control, like Markdown content coming from a database or API and rendered to HTML.
>
> ### With arbitrary values
>
> Using theme variables in arbitrary values can be useful, especially in combination with the `calc()` function.
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:rounded-xl] -->
> <div class="relative rounded-xl">
>   <!-- [!code word:rounded-\[calc(var(--radius-xl)-1px)\]] -->
>   <div class="absolute inset-px rounded-[calc(var(--radius-xl)-1px)]">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
>   <!-- ... -->
> </div>
> ```
>
> In the above example, we're subtracting 1px from the `--radius-xl` value on a nested inset element to make sure it has a concentric border radius.
>
> ### Referencing in JavaScript
>
> Most of the time when you need to reference your theme variables in JS you can just use the CSS variables directly, just like any other CSS value.
>
> For example, the popular [Motion](https://motion.dev/docs/react-quick-start) library for React lets you animate to and from CSS variable values:
>
> ```jsx
> // [!code filename:JSX]
> // [!code word:var(--color-blue-500)]
> <motion.div animate={{ backgroundColor: "var(--color-blue-500)" }} />
> ```
>
> If you need access to a resolved CSS variable value in JS, you can use `getComputedStyle` to get the value of a theme variable on the document root:
>
> ```js
> // [!code filename:spaghetti.js]
> let styles = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement);
> let shadow = styles.getPropertyValue("--shadow-xl");
> ```
>
>
>

> ## Upgrade Guide > Changes from v3 > Default border color
> Upgrade Guide | tailwindcss@4.x | Source: https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss.com/blob/main/src/docs/upgrade-guide.mdx
>
> ### Default border color
>
> In v3, the `border-*` and `divide-*` utilities used your configured `gray-200` color by default. We've changed this to `currentColor` in v4 to make Tailwind less opinionated and match browser defaults.
>
> To update your project for this change, make sure you specify a color anywhere you're using a `border-*` or `divide-*` utility:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code classes:border-gray-200] -->
> <div class="border border-gray-200 px-2 py-3 ...">
>   <!-- ... -->
> </div>
> ```
>
> Alternatively, add these base styles to your project to preserve the v3 behavior:
>
> ```css
> /* [!code filename:CSS] */
> @layer base {
>   *,
>   ::after,
>   ::before,
>   ::backdrop,
>   ::file-selector-button {
>     border-color: var(--color-gray-200, currentColor);
>   }
> }
> ```
>

- Creator and product cards now use system `rounded-card` tokens.
- Added subtle glass surfaces with semantic colors.
- Avatar overlaps the cover; name and profile title sit beside it.

> ## Validation Form Request Validation Creating Form Requests
> Validation | laravel/framework@12.x | Source: https://github.com/laravel/docs/blob/12.x/validation.md
>
> <a name="creating-form-requests"></a>
> ### Creating Form Requests
>
> For more complex validation scenarios, you may wish to create a "form request". Form requests are custom request classes that encapsulate their own validation and authorization logic. To create a form request class, you may use the `make:request` Artisan CLI command:
>
> ```shell
> php artisan make:request StorePostRequest
> ```
>
> The generated form request class will be placed in the `app/Http/Requests` directory. If this directory does not exist, it will be created when you run the `make:request` command. Each form request generated by Laravel has two methods: `authorize` and `rules`.
>
> As you might have guessed, the `authorize` method is responsible for determining if the currently authenticated user can perform the action represented by the request, while the `rules` method returns the validation rules that should apply to the request's data:
>
> ```php
> /**
>  * Get the validation rules that apply to the request.
>  *
>  * @return array<string, \Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\ValidationRule|array<mixed>|string>
>  */
> public function rules(): array
> {
>     return [
>         'title' => 'required|unique:posts|max:255',
>         'body' => 'required',
>     ];
> }
> ```
>
> > [!NOTE]
> > You may type-hint any dependencies you require within the `rules` method's signature. They will automatically be resolved via the Laravel [service container](/docs/{{version}}/container).
>
> So, how are the validation rules evaluated? All you need to do is type-hint the request on your controller method. The incoming form request is validated before the controller method is called, meaning you do not need to clutter your controller with any validation logic:
>
> ```php
> /**
>  * Store a new blog post.
>  */
> public function store(StorePostRequest $request): RedirectResponse
> {
>     // The incoming request is valid...
>
>     // Retrieve the validated input data...
>     $validated = $request->validated();
>
>     // Retrieve a portion of the validated input data...
>     $validated = $request->safe()->only(['name', 'email']);
>     $validated = $request->safe()->except(['name', 'email']);
>
>     // Store the blog post...
>
>     return redirect('/posts');
> }
> ```
>
> If validation fails, a redirect response will be generated to send the user back to their previous location. The errors will also be flashed to the session so they are available for display. If the request was an XHR request, an HTTP response with a 422 status code will be returned to the user including a [JSON representation of the validation errors](#validation-error-response-format).
>
> > [!NOTE]
> > Need to add real-time form request validation to your Inertia powered Laravel frontend? Check out [Laravel Precognition](/docs/{{version}}/precognition).
>

> <a name="validation-assert-invalid"></a>
> #### assertInvalid
>
> Assert that the response has validation errors for the given keys. This method may be used for asserting against responses where the validation errors are returned as a JSON structure or where the validation errors have been flashed to the session:
>
> ```php
> $response->assertInvalid(['name', 'email']);
> ```
>
> You may also assert that a given key has a particular validation error message. When doing so, you may provide the entire message or only a small portion of the message:
>
> ```php
> $response->assertInvalid([
>     'name' => 'The name field is required.',
>     'email' => 'valid email address',
> ]);
> ```

> ## Validation Custom Validation Rules Implicit Rules
> Validation | laravel/framework@12.x | Source: https://github.com/laravel/docs/blob/12.x/validation.md
>
> <a name="implicit-rules"></a>
> ### Implicit Rules
>
> By default, when an attribute being validated is not present or contains an empty string, normal validation rules, including custom rules, are not run. For example, the [unique](#rule-unique) rule will not be run against an empty string:
>
> ```php
> use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Validator;
>
> $rules = ['name' => 'unique:users,name'];
>
> $input = ['name' => ''];
>
> Validator::make($input, $rules)->passes(); // true
> ```
>
> For a custom rule to run even when an attribute is empty, the rule must imply that the attribute is required. To quickly generate a new implicit rule object, you may use the `make:rule` Artisan command with the `--implicit` option:
>
> ```shell
> php artisan make:rule Uppercase --implicit
> ```
>
> > [!WARNING]
> > An "implicit" rule only _implies_ that the attribute is required. Whether it actually invalidates a missing or empty attribute is up to you.
>

> #### Customizing the Validation Attributes
>
> Many of Laravel's built-in validation rule error messages contain an `:attribute` placeholder. If you would like the `:attribute` placeholder of your validation message to be replaced with a custom attribute name, you may specify the custom names by overriding the `attributes` method. This method should return an array of attribute / name pairs:

> ```php
> /**
>  * Get custom attributes for validator errors.
>  *
>  * @return array<string, string>
>  */
> public function attributes(): array
> {
>     return [
>         'email' => 'email address',
>     ];
> }
> ```

> ## Precognition Customizing Validation Rules
> Precognition | laravel/framework@12.x | Source: https://github.com/laravel/docs/blob/12.x/precognition.md
>
> <a name="customizing-validation-rules"></a>
> ## Customizing Validation Rules
>
> It is possible to customize the validation rules executed during a precognitive request by using the request's `isPrecognitive` method.
>
> For example, on a user creation form, we may want to validate that a password is "uncompromised" only on the final form submission. For precognitive validation requests, we will simply validate that the password is required and has a minimum of 8 characters. Using the `isPrecognitive` method, we can customize the rules defined by our form request:
>
> ```php
> <?php
>
> namespace App\Http\Requests;
>
> use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;
> use Illuminate\Validation\Rules\Password;
>
> class StoreUserRequest extends FormRequest
> {
>     /**
>      * Get the validation rules that apply to the request.
>      *
>      * @return array
>      */
>     protected function rules()
>     {
>         return [
>             'password' => [
>                 'required',
>                 $this->isPrecognitive()
>                     ? Password::min(8)
>                     : Password::min(8)->uncompromised(),
>             ],
>             // ...
>         ];
>     }
> }
> ```
>
> ---
>
> ## Validation Custom Validation Rules Using Rule Objects
> Validation | laravel/framework@12.x | Source: https://github.com/laravel/docs/blob/12.x/validation.md
>
> <a name="using-rule-objects"></a>
> ### Using Rule Objects
>
> Laravel provides a variety of helpful validation rules; however, you may wish to specify some of your own. One method of registering custom validation rules is using rule objects. To generate a new rule object, you may use the `make:rule` Artisan command. Let's use this command to generate a rule that verifies a string is uppercase. Laravel will place the new rule in the `app/Rules` directory. If this directory does not exist, Laravel will create it when you execute the Artisan command to create your rule:
>
> ```shell
> php artisan make:rule Uppercase
> ```
>
> Once the rule has been created, we are ready to define its behavior. A rule object contains a single method: `validate`. This method receives the attribute name, its value, and a callback that should be invoked on failure with the validation error message:
>
> ```php
> <?php
>
> namespace App\Rules;
>
> use Closure;
> use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\ValidationRule;
>
> class Uppercase implements ValidationRule
> {
>     /**
>      * Run the validation rule.
>      */
>     public function validate(string $attribute, mixed $value, Closure $fail): void
>     {
>         if (strtoupper($value) !== $value) {
>             $fail('The :attribute must be uppercase.');
>         }
>     }
> }
> ```
>
> Once the rule has been defined, you may attach it to a validator by passing an instance of the rule object with your other validation rules:
>
> ```php
> use App\Rules\Uppercase;
>
> $request->validate([
>     'name' => ['required', 'string', new Uppercase],
> ]);
> ```
>
> #### Translating Validation Messages
>
> Instead of providing a literal error message to the `$fail` closure, you may also provide a [translation string key](/docs/{{version}}/localization) and instruct Laravel to translate the error message:
>
> ```php
> if (strtoupper($value) !== $value) {
>     $fail('validation.uppercase')->translate();
> }
> ```
>
> If necessary, you may provide placeholder replacements and the preferred language as the first and second arguments to the `translate` method:
>
> ```php
> $fail('validation.location')->translate([
>     'value' => $this->value,
> ], 'fr');
> ```
>
> #### Accessing Additional Data
>
> If your custom validation rule class needs to access all of the other data undergoing validation, your rule class may implement the `Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\DataAwareRule` interface. This interface requires your class to define a `setData` method. This method will automatically be invoked by Laravel (before validation proceeds) with all of the data under validation:
>
> ```php
> <?php
>
> namespace App\Rules;
>
> use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\DataAwareRule;
> use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\ValidationRule;
>
> class Uppercase implements DataAwareRule, ValidationRule
> {
>     /**
>      * All of the data under validation.
>      *
>      * @var array<string, mixed>
>      */
>     protected $data = [];
>
>     // ...
>
>     /**
>      * Set the data under validation.
>      *
>      * @param  array<string, mixed>  $data
>      */
>     public function setData(array $data): static
>     {
>         $this->data = $data;
>
>         return $this;
>     }
> }
> ```
>
> Or, if your validation rule requires access to the validator instance performing the validation, you may implement the `ValidatorAwareRule` interface:
>
> ```php
> <?php
>
> namespace App\Rules;
>
> use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\ValidationRule;
> use Illuminate\Contracts\Validation\ValidatorAwareRule;
> use Illuminate\Validation\Validator;
>
> class Uppercase implements ValidationRule, ValidatorAwareRule
> {
>     /**
>      * The validator instance.
>      *
>      * @var \Illuminate\Validation\Validator
>      */
>     protected $validator;
>
>     // ...
>
>     /**
>      * Set the current validator.
>      */
>     public function setValidator(Validator $validator): static
>     {
>         $this->validator = $validator;
>
>         return $this;
>     }
> }
> ```

Fixed the Creator Profile save error.

Cause: Linket uploads images as relative paths such as `storage/link-images/...`, but validation previously required absolute HTTP URLs.

Now:

- Owned avatar and cover uploads save correctly.
- External HTTP/HTTPS images still work.
- Missing files and another creator’s uploads are rejected.
- Tests: 10 passed, 45 assertions.
- PHPStan: no errors.

Updated [UpdateCreatorProfileRequest.php](./app/Biolinks/Requests/UpdateCreatorProfileRequest.php) and its tests.

Refresh the builder page, then click **Save changes** again.

> # Search Results

> ## Responsive Design Container queries
> Responsive Design | tailwindcss@4.x | Source: https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss.com/blob/main/src/docs/responsive-design.mdx
>
> ## Container queries
>
> ### What are container queries?
>
> [Container queries](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries) are a modern CSS feature that let you style something based on the size of a parent element instead of the size of the entire viewport. They let you build components that are a lot more portable and reusable because they can change based on the actual space available for that component.
>
> ### Basic example
>
> Use the `@container` class to mark an element as an inline-size container, then use variants like `@sm` and `@md` to style child elements based on the size of the container:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@container] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@md\:flex-row] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-col @md:flex-row">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> Just like breakpoint variants, container queries are mobile-first in Tailwind CSS and apply at the target container size and up.
>
> ### Max-width container queries
>
> Use variants like `@max-sm` and `@max-md` to apply a style below a specific container size:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@max-md\:flex-col] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-row @max-md:flex-col">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Container query ranges
>
> Stack a regular container query variant with a max-width container query variant to target a specific range:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@sm\:@max-md\:flex-col] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-row @sm:@max-md:flex-col">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Named containers
>
> For complex designs that use multiple nested containers, you can name containers using `@container/{name}` and target specific containers with variants like `@sm/{name}` and `@md/{name}`:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@container/main] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@sm/main\:flex-col] -->
> <div class="@container/main">
>   <!-- ... -->
>   <div class="flex flex-row @sm/main:flex-col">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> This makes it possible to style something based on the size of a distant container, rather than just the nearest container.
>
> ### Using size containers
>
> Use `@container-size` to mark an element as a size container instead of an inline-size container when you need to use container query length units that depend on the block size, like `cqb`:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@container-size] -->
> <!-- [!code word:h-\[50cqb\]] -->
> <div class="@container-size">
>   <div class="h-[50cqb]">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> You can also name size containers using `@container-size/{name}`.
>
> ### Using custom container sizes
>
> Use the `--container-*` theme variables to customize your container sizes:
>
> ```css
> /* [!code filename:app.css] */
> @import "tailwindcss";
>
> @theme {
>   /* [!code highlight:2] */
>   --container-8xl: 96rem;
> }
> ```
>
> This adds a new `8xl` container query variant that can be used in your markup:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@8xl\:flex-row] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <!-- prettier-ignore -->
>   <div class="flex flex-col @8xl:flex-row">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> Learn more about customizing your theme in the [theme documentation](/docs/theme).
>
> <h3 id="using-arbitrary-container-query-values">
>   Using arbitrary values
> </h3>
>
> Use variants like `@min-[475px]` and `@max-[960px]` for one-off container query sizes you don't want to add to your theme:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@min-\[475px\]\:flex-row] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-col @min-[475px]:flex-row">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Using container query units
>
> Use [container query length units](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries#container_query_length_units) like `cqw` and `cqi` as arbitrary values in other utility classes to reference the container size:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:w-\[50cqw\]] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="w-[50cqw]">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> For units that need more than the inline size, like `cqb` and `cqh`, use `@container-size` to make the full size of the container available.
>

> ### What are container queries?
>
> [Container queries](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries) are a modern CSS feature that let you style something based on the size of a parent element instead of the size of the entire viewport. They let you build components that are a lot more portable and reusable because they can change based on the actual space available for that component.
>
> ### Basic example
>
> Use the `@container` class to mark an element as an inline-size container, then use variants like `@sm` and `@md` to style child elements based on the size of the container:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@container] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@md\:flex-row] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-col @md:flex-row">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> Just like breakpoint variants, container queries are mobile-first in Tailwind CSS and apply at the target container size and up.
>
> ### Max-width container queries
>
> Use variants like `@max-sm` and `@max-md` to apply a style below a specific container size:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@max-md\:flex-col] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-row @max-md:flex-col">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Container query ranges
>
> Stack a regular container query variant with a max-width container query variant to target a specific range:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@sm\:@max-md\:flex-col] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-row @sm:@max-md:flex-col">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Named containers
>
> For complex designs that use multiple nested containers, you can name containers using `@container/{name}` and target specific containers with variants like `@sm/{name}` and `@md/{name}`:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@container/main] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@sm/main\:flex-col] -->
> <div class="@container/main">
>   <!-- ... -->
>   <div class="flex flex-row @sm/main:flex-col">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> This makes it possible to style something based on the size of a distant container, rather than just the nearest container.
>
> ### Using size containers
>
> Use `@container-size` to mark an element as a size container instead of an inline-size container when you need to use container query length units that depend on the block size, like `cqb`:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@container-size] -->
> <!-- [!code word:h-\[50cqb\]] -->
> <div class="@container-size">
>   <div class="h-[50cqb]">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> You can also name size containers using `@container-size/{name}`.
>
> ### Using custom container sizes
>
> Use the `--container-*` theme variables to customize your container sizes:
>
> ```css
> /* [!code filename:app.css] */
> @import "tailwindcss";
>
> @theme {
>   /* [!code highlight:2] */
>   --container-8xl: 96rem;
> }
> ```
>
> This adds a new `8xl` container query variant that can be used in your markup:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@8xl\:flex-row] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <!-- prettier-ignore -->
>   <div class="flex flex-col @8xl:flex-row">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> Learn more about customizing your theme in the [theme documentation](/docs/theme).
>
> <h3 id="using-arbitrary-container-query-values">
>   Using arbitrary values
> </h3>
>
> Use variants like `@min-[475px]` and `@max-[960px]` for one-off container query sizes you don't want to add to your theme:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:@min-\[475px\]\:flex-row] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="flex flex-col @min-[475px]:flex-row">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Using container query units
>
> Use [container query length units](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries#container_query_length_units) like `cqw` and `cqi` as arbitrary values in other utility classes to reference the container size:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- [!code word:w-\[50cqw\]] -->
> <div class="@container">
>   <div class="w-[50cqw]">
>     <!-- ... -->
>   </div>
> </div>
> ```
>
> For units that need more than the inline size, like `cqb` and `cqh`, use `@container-size` to make the full size of the container available.
>

>

>
> ### Using a percentage
>
> Use `max-w-full` or `max-w-<fraction>` utilities like `max-w-1/2` and `max-w-2/5` to give an element a percentage-based maximum width:
>
> <Figure hint="Resize the example to see the expected behavior">

>
> ```html

> <div class="w-full max-w-3/4 ...">max-w-3/4</div>
> <div class="w-full max-w-1/2 ...">max-w-1/2</div>
> <div class="w-full max-w-1/3 ...">max-w-1/3</div>
> ```
>
> </Figure>
>
> ### Using the container scale
>
> Use utilities like `max-w-sm` and `max-w-xl` to set an element to a fixed maximum width based on the container scale:

> ```html
> <!-- [!code classes:max-w-md] -->
> <div class="max-w-md ...">
>   <!-- ... -->
> </div>
> ```
>
> </Figure>
>
> ### Using breakpoints container
>
> Use the `container` utility to set the maximum width of an element to match the `min-width` of the current breakpoint. This is useful if you'd prefer to design for a fixed set of screen sizes instead of trying to accommodate a fully fluid viewport:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code classes:container] -->
> <div class="container">
>   <!-- ... -->
> </div>
> ```
>
> Note that unlike containers you might have used in other frameworks, Tailwind's container does not center itself automatically and does not have any built-in horizontal padding. Use `mx-auto` and the `px-<number>` utilities to add these:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code classes:mx-auto,px-4] -->
> <div class="container mx-auto px-4">
>   <!-- ... -->
> </div>
> ```
>
> ### Using a custom value
>
> <UsingACustomValue utility="max-w" value="220px" name="maximum width" variable="max-width" />
>
> ### Responsive design
>
> <ResponsiveDesign property="max-width" defaultClass="max-w-sm" featuredClass="max-w-lg" />
>

> # Search Results

> ## Styling With Utility Classes > Thinking in utility classes > When to use inline styles
> Styling With Utility Classes | tailwindcss@4.x | Source: https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss.com/blob/main/src/docs/styling-with-utility-classes.mdx
>
> ### When to use inline styles
>
> Inline styles are still very useful in Tailwind CSS projects, particularly when a value is coming from a dynamic source like a database or API:
>
> ```jsx
> // [!code filename:branded-button.jsx]
> export function BrandedButton({ buttonColor, textColor, children }) {
>   return (
>     <button
>       style={{
>         // [!code highlight:3]
>         backgroundColor: buttonColor,
>         color: textColor,
>       }}
>       className="rounded-md px-3 py-1.5 font-medium"
>     >
>       {children}
>     </button>
>   );
> }
> ```
>
> You might also reach for an inline style for very complicated arbitrary values that are difficult to read when formatted as a class name:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML] -->
> <!-- prettier-ignore -->
> <div class="grid-[2fr_max(0,var(--gutter-width))_calc(var(--gutter-width)+10px)]"> <!-- [!code --] -->
> <!-- prettier-ignore -->
> <div style="grid-template-columns: 2fr max(0, var(--gutter-width)) calc(var(--gutter-width) + 10px)"> <!-- [!code ++] -->
>   <!-- ... -->
> </div>
> ```
>
> Another useful pattern is setting CSS variables based on dynamic sources using inline styles, then referencing those variables with utility classes:
>
> ```jsx
> // [!code filename:branded-button.jsx]
> export function BrandedButton({ buttonColor, buttonColorHover, textColor, children }) {
>   return (
>     <button
>       style={{
>         // [!code highlight:4]
>         "--bg-color": buttonColor,
>         "--bg-color-hover": buttonColorHover,
>         "--text-color": textColor,
>       }}
>       // [!code classes:bg-(--bg-color),text-(--text-color),hover:bg-(--bg-color-hover)]
>       className="bg-(--bg-color) text-(--text-color) hover:bg-(--bg-color-hover) ..."
>     >
>       {children}
>     </button>
>   );
> }
> ```
>
> ---

> ## Responsive Design Overview
> Responsive Design | tailwindcss@4.x | Source: https://github.com/tailwindlabs/tailwindcss.com/blob/main/src/docs/responsive-design.mdx
>
> ## Overview
>
> Every utility class in Tailwind can be applied conditionally at different breakpoints, which makes it a piece of cake to build complex responsive interfaces without ever leaving your HTML.
>
> First, make sure you've added the [viewport meta tag](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Viewport_meta_tag) to the `<head>` of your document:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:index.html] -->
> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
> ```
>
> Then to add a utility but only have it take effect at a certain breakpoint, all you need to do is prefix the utility with the breakpoint name, followed by the `:` character:
>
> ```html
> <!-- [!code filename:HTML]  -->
> <!-- [!code word:md\:w-32] -->
> <!-- [!code word:lg\:w-48] -->
> <!-- Width of 16 by default, 32 on medium screens, and 48 on large screens -->
> <img class="w-16 md:w-32 lg:w-48" src="..." />
> ```
>
> There are five breakpoints by default, inspired by common device resolutions:
>
> {
>
> <table>
>   <thead>
>     <tr>
>       <th>Breakpoint prefix</th>
>       <th>Minimum width</th>
>       <th>CSS</th>
>     </tr>
>   </thead>
>   <tbody>
>     <tr>
>       <td>
>         <code>sm</code>
>       </td>
>       <td>
>         40rem <em>(640px)</em>
>       </td>
>       <td>
>         <code>@media (width &gt;= 40rem) &#123; ... &#125;</code>
>       </td>
>     </tr>
>     <tr>
>       <td>
>         <code>md</code>
>       </td>
>       <td>
>         48rem <em>(768px)</em>
>       </td>
>       <td>

>
> This works for **every utility class in the framework**, which means you can change literally anything at a given breakpoint — even things like letter spacing or cursor styles.
>
> Here's a simple example of a marketing page component that uses a stacked layout on small screens, and a side-by-side layout on larger screens:
>
> <Figure>
>
> <Example resizable padding={false}>

> ```html
> <!-- [!code word:md\:max-w-2xl] -->
> <div class="mx-auto max-w-md overflow-hidden rounded-xl bg-white shadow-md md:max-w-2xl">

>   <div class="md:flex">
>     <!-- [!code word:md\:shrink-0] -->

>       <!-- [!code word:md\:h-full] -->
>       <!-- [!code word:md\:w-48] -->

>
> Here's how the example above works:
>
> - By default, the outer `div` is `display: block`, but by adding the `md:flex` utility, it becomes `display: flex` on medium screens and larger.
> - When the parent is a flex container, we want to make sure the image never shrinks, so we've added `md:shrink-0` to prevent shrinking on medium screens and larger. Technically we could have just used `shrink-0` since it would do nothing on smaller screens, but since it only matters on `md` screens, it's a good idea to make that clear in the class name.
> - On small screens the image is automatically full width by default. On medium screens and up, we've constrained the width to a fixed size and ensured the image is full height using `md:h-full md:w-48`.
>
> We've only used one breakpoint in this example, but you could easily customize this component at other sizes using the `sm`, `lg`, `xl`, or `2xl` responsive prefixes as well.

>
> Plan
>
> # Digital Creator Storefront MVP
>
> ## Summary
>
> Build a workspace-owned digital-download marketplace that lets creators add approved products to a Shop widget on their biolink page, take one-time Stripe payments, and deliver protected downloads. Keep it separate from the existing subscription-plan `Product` models.
>
> ## Implementation changes
>
> - Add a dedicated storefront domain with `DigitalProduct`, product files/previews, `Order`, `OrderItem`, `DownloadEntitlement`, and `PayoutRequest` records.
>   - Products belong to the active workspace/creator and support `draft`, `pending_approval`, `approved`, `rejected`, and `archived` states.
>   - Orders snapshot price, currency, creator commission rate, platform fee, creator earnings, and Stripe IDs so later plan changes do not alter completed sales.
>   - Reuse existing file-entry uploads, but enforce configurable size limits and a safe downloadable-file allowlist.
>
> - Add configurable storefront benefits to each subscription plan: product quota, commission rate, and maximum upload size.
>   - Default mapping: Free = 7 products / 10%; Pro = 50 / 5%; Business = unlimited / 2%.
>   - Admins map these benefits to actual plan records rather than relying on plan names.
>
> - Add creator dashboard pages for product management, sales/earnings, and payout requests.
>   - Creators create products with title, description, price, cover image, and downloadable files.
>   - Submitting sends the product to admin review; only approved products can appear publicly.
>   - Earnings show gross sales, platform commission, pending payout balance, and paid balance.
>
> - Add admin screens for product approval and payout requests.
>   - Admins approve/reject listings with an optional reason.
>   - Admins review payout requests and mark them paid after completing the transfer outside Linket.
>   - Refunds and disputes remain in the Stripe Dashboard for this MVP.
>
> - Add a Shop widget to the existing biolink widget registry.
>   - A creator selects approved products from their workspace and configures the widget title/layout.
>   - Public biolink pages render product cards; product details open in-app and begin checkout.
>   - Use the existing appearance configuration so the widget inherits the creator’s biolink styling.
>
> - Add a one-time Stripe Checkout flow.
>   - Create a hosted Checkout Session for a selected approved product and redirect back to a Linket confirmation page.
>   - Verify signed Stripe webhooks and handle them idempotently to create paid orders and download entitlements.
>   - Email a receipt and display a signed download link valid for 7 days and limited to 10 downloads.
>   - Do not enable Stripe Tax or configure payment methods explicitly; use the platform currency and Stripe’s dynamic payment methods.
>
> ## Public interfaces and safeguards
>
> - Add creator/admin API resources for products, sales summaries, payout requests, approval actions, checkout-session creation, and protected download retrieval.
> - Add a public product-detail/checkout route scoped to the creator’s biolink and an entitlement-based download endpoint.
> - Enforce workspace ownership, product quotas, approval status, file ownership, signed URL expiry, download count, webhook signature validation, and webhook idempotency.
> - Queue receipt emails and any non-blocking file-processing work.
>
> ## Test plan
>
> - Product quota and upload-limit enforcement for Free, Pro, and Business plan settings.
> - Creator/admin authorization and approval-state transitions.
> - Public widget shows only approved products selected for that biolink.
> - Checkout session creation rejects unpublished, unauthorized, or unavailable products.
> - Stripe webhook creates exactly one completed order when delivered repeatedly.
> - Correct fee/earnings snapshots for 10%, 5%, and 2% commissions.
> - Download links work only for paid orders, expire after seven days, and stop after ten uses.
> - Payout requests use only available unpaid earnings and cannot be duplicated beyond the available balance.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - MVP sells one-time downloadable files only; services, subscriptions, coupons, order bumps, PayPal checkout, Stripe Connect, automatic payouts, refunds, disputes, and multi-currency are deferred.
> - Products belong to the active workspace and can be selected by one or more biolink Shop widgets in that workspace.
> - The pricing scope defaults to one configured platform currency with tax collection disabled until tax registrations are configured.
</details>

The database inspection did not return within the safe read-only window, so I’ll make the plan independent of any specific existing plan IDs: the admin will map each plan to its product quota, commission, and upload limit. One final commerce decision affects pricing, checkout configuration, and receipts.

> Plan

> # Digital Products: Product-First Creator Storefront
>
> ## Summary
>
> Replace the current sales-first storefront dashboard with a clean shadcn-based creator experience:
>
> - `/dashboard/my-products` — create, edit, submit, and assign digital products to bio pages.
> - `/dashboard/sales-payouts` — sales, earnings, payout requests, and withdrawal-method settings.
> - `/admin/storefront` — separate admin controls for product approval and payout processing.
>
> This milestone uses and improves the existing storefront MVP APIs. Checkout, Stripe webhooks, protected downloads, and automated payouts are not expanded.
>
> ## Creator UI and navigation
>
> - Add **Digital Products** and **Sales & Payouts** to the dashboard menu, including a safe settings backfill so existing installations receive the links without duplicating them.
> - Rebuild `/dashboard/my-products` as a product catalog with quota usage, status filters, product cards/table, empty state, and clear actions for create, edit, submit for approval, and delete.
> - Add dedicated create/edit routes with shadcn form controls:
>   - title, description, price, cover upload, downloadable-file uploads, status/rejection feedback;
>   - direct uploads inside the form using Linket’s upload provider, storefront file restrictions, and progress/error states;
>   - save as draft or submit for approval.
> - Add a **Show on bio pages** multi-select to each product. A creator selects one or more workspace bio pages from the product form.
> - Build `/dashboard/sales-payouts` separately from product management. It will show earnings cards, completed sales, payout history, available balance, a payout-request dialog, and a withdrawal-method card.
> - Add a basic manual withdrawal-method form: bank transfer, PayPal, or other; account holder and payout destination are stored encrypted, displayed masked, and used only by admins for manual payouts. No Stripe Connect, automatic transfers, or card details.
>
> ## Bio page Shop behavior
>
> - Make product-to-bio-page assignment the source of truth with a `digital_product_biolinks` relationship.
> - Extend product create/update responses and requests with assigned `biolink_ids`; validate that every selected bio page belongs to the active workspace.
> - When a product is assigned to a bio page, create one managed Shop widget on that page if needed. Products assigned to that page appear in its Shop widget.
> - Replace the current manual “Product IDs” field in the Shop widget dialog. It will only configure presentation: title and layout. Product membership is managed from the product edit screen.
> - Removing the last assigned product removes only an empty auto-managed Shop widget; creator-configured title/layout remains when products still exist.
> - Update public Shop rendering to request products by biolink, show only approved products with covers and prices, open a product-detail dialog, and start the existing checkout flow.
>
> ## Admin controls and backend wiring
>
> - Add `/admin/storefront/products` for pending-product review, with product details, downloadable-file metadata, approve, and reject-with-reason actions.
> - Add `/admin/storefront/payouts` for payout requests, masked withdrawal details, and manual “mark paid” processing.
> - Protect all storefront admin routes and APIs with admin permission checks; retain workspace and creator ownership checks for creator endpoints.
> - Add payout-method storage and snapshot the selected masked payout destination onto each payout request so later changes do not alter a request already being processed.
> - Keep all UI components within Linket’s shadcn component system, use Lucide icons, `Trans` text, design tokens, responsive layouts, and non-overlapping dialogs/sheets.
>
> ## Test plan
>
> - Creator can only manage products, files, bio pages, payout methods, and payout requests in their active workspace.
> - Product create/edit validates upload restrictions, quotas, visibility selections, and approval-state transitions.
> - Assigning/removing products correctly creates, updates, or removes managed Shop widgets.
> - Public bio pages expose only approved products assigned to that specific page.
> - Creator Sales & Payouts accurately reflects existing paid orders and prevents requests above available earnings.
> - Withdrawal details are encrypted/masked and payout requests retain the selected destination snapshot.
> - Admin-only approval and payout actions reject creator access.
> - Run Laravel tests, API schema generation/type generation as applicable, and a production frontend build; manually verify responsive creator, bio-page, and admin flows.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Products are assigned to bio pages from the product create/edit screen and may appear on multiple pages.
> - Digital Products and Sales & Payouts are separate creator sidebar pages.
> - Withdrawal methods support manual off-platform payouts only; Linket will not automatically move money in this milestone.
> - Existing Stripe Checkout, webhook, receipt, and download-entitlement behavior remains unchanged.
</details>

Because the payout screen affects payment and personal financial details, I’m applying the project’s Stripe-integration guidance to keep the “withdrawal method” limited to safe manual-payout instructions in this milestone—no automatic transfers or new checkout behavior.

> Plan
>
> # Public Digital Products Buying Flow
>
> ## Summary
>
> Complete the customer journey: approved products appear on their selected bio pages, open a branded product page, launch Stripe Checkout, then show protected downloads after the webhook confirms payment. Product pages will match the bio page appearance chosen by the creator.
>
> ## Implementation Changes
>
> - Add canonical public routes before the short-link fallback:
>   - `/{biolink}/products/{digitalProduct}` — product detail page.
>   - `/{biolink}/products/{digitalProduct}/orders/{order}/success` — payment confirmation page.
>   - Generate these URLs from the selected bio page’s existing `short_url`, including custom domains.
> - Create a public product-page loader and React screens that reuse the bio page’s fonts/background/appearance without rendering the full bio page:
>   - Product cover, title, description, price, creator context, and a single clear “Buy now” action.
>   - Checkout cancel returns to the product page with a small inline status message.
>   - Success page shows “Finalizing payment” while pending, refreshes order state, and exposes download buttons only once payment is confirmed.
> - Replace the Shop widget’s direct checkout action:
>   - Load only approved products attached to the current bio page.
>   - Product cards open the canonical product-detail URL.
>   - Keep widget settings limited to title and layout; Digital Products remains the source of product assignment.
> - Add bio-page-scoped public APIs:
>   - `GET /api/v1/public/biolinks/{biolink}/digital-products`
>   - `GET /api/v1/public/biolinks/{biolink}/digital-products/{digitalProduct}`
>   - `POST /api/v1/public/biolinks/{biolink}/digital-products/{digitalProduct}/checkout`
>   - Validate that the bio page is publicly accessible, the product is approved, belongs to that page, and has downloadable files.
>   - Keep existing unscoped `storefront` and `digital-products` public endpoints only as temporary compatibility aliases while the frontend moves.
> - Extend checkout order context with the originating bio page so the success page can validate and retain the correct branded placement. Legacy orders remain readable.
> - Update the existing Checkout session URLs to use the new product and order routes. Continue using hosted Stripe Checkout, dynamic payment methods, server-only Stripe credentials, and no Stripe Tax configuration.
> - Keep signed webhook verification and idempotent fulfillment; additionally handle delayed-payment success events so dynamic payment methods can still fulfill correctly. The redirect never grants downloads by itself.
> - Preserve the queued receipt email and protected entitlement links: seven-day expiry, ten-download limit, and no direct file URLs.
> - Finish the existing admin queue rather than creating a parallel system:

>   - Approve or reject with a reason; only approved products become available through the public bio-page APIs.
>
> ## UI Direction
>

> - Protected downloads still expire after seven days and stop after ten downloads.
> - Admin-only approval/rejection controls determine public visibility.

> ## Assumptions

> - Refunds, disputes, Stripe Connect, automatic payouts, and multi-currency remain out of scope.

> # Chapa-First Payments for Linket
>
> ## Summary
>
> Make Chapa the only gateway for all new payments: Digital Products and subscription plans use hosted Chapa checkout in ETB. Existing Stripe/PayPal orders and subscriptions remain valid through their paid period, then renew through Chapa. No amount is silently converted from USD to ETB.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Install `chapa/chapa-laravel` and add server-only Chapa settings (`CHAPA_SECRET_KEY`, enabled state). Replace the active payment-gateway controls with a Chapa section; keep Stripe/PayPal credentials and webhook routes only for legacy payments.
> - Add a gateway-neutral `payment_transactions` record for Chapa attempts, with a unique `tx_ref`, billable target (subscription or digital-product order), expected ETB amount, status, verified Chapa transaction ID, and sanitized verification metadata.
> - Add a signed Chapa webhook/callback endpoint. Validate `x-chapa-signature`, then verify the transaction server-to-server and require an exact match on `tx_ref`, amount, currency, and target before marking anything paid. Callback and webhook handling must be idempotent.
> - Update Digital Products checkout:
>   - The existing public checkout API creates a pending order and Chapa hosted-payment URL.
>   - Product success pages use `tx_ref`, show a processing state, and poll order status.
>   - Downloads, receipts, creator earnings, and payout balances are created only after verified payment.
>   - Existing Stripe-paid orders, receipts, and download entitlements keep working.
> - Update subscription checkout:
>   - New subscriptions and renewals open Chapa hosted checkout; remove Stripe Elements, stored-card, and PayPal controls from new checkout.
>   - Chapa subscriptions renew manually every billing period: reminders at 7, 3, and 1 days before renewal; a 7-day grace period after due date; access ends if no verified payment arrives.
>   - Cancellation keeps access through the paid period. Plan changes take effect at the next renewal—no proration, refunds, or automatic charges.
>   - Trials continue until their scheduled end, then prompt the user to pay through Chapa.
>   - Paid Chapa renewals update the subscription, create invoices/payment history, and restore access atomically.
> - Enforce ETB for all new subscription prices and Digital Product prices. Existing USD records remain historically accurate but cannot start a Chapa payment until an admin or creator manually enters an ETB price.
> - Preserve the manual creator payout workflow. Chapa transfers, subaccounts, automatic payouts, and Stripe Connect remain out of scope.
>
> ## Interfaces and Security
>
> - Add Chapa checkout/status endpoints for authenticated subscription purchase and renewal flows.
> - Keep the bio-page-scoped Digital Products checkout endpoint, but return a Chapa checkout URL instead of a Stripe session URL.
> - Add the Chapa webhook route under billing webhooks; exempt only that external webhook/callback route from CSRF.
> - Use rate limiting for checkout creation, never expose Chapa keys to the browser, and log rejected signatures or verification mismatches without logging secrets.
> - Retain legacy Stripe/PayPal webhook handling until every legacy active subscription has ended or moved to Chapa.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - Chapa checkout creation uses ETB, a unique reference, correct amount, return URL, and callback URL.
> - Invalid webhook signatures, failed verification, mismatched amount/currency/reference, and duplicate events never grant access.
> - A verified Chapa Digital Product payment creates one paid order, entitlements, receipt, sales totals, and payout balance.
> - Product success pages never expose downloads until verified payment completes.
> - Subscription initial purchase, renewal reminders, grace expiry, cancellation, trial expiry, and next-period plan changes behave correctly.
> - USD legacy prices cannot create Chapa payments; manually configured ETB prices can.
> - Legacy Stripe/PayPal subscriptions and paid Digital Product downloads remain readable during migration.
> - Run PHPUnit, PHPStan, generated API types, and the production frontend build.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Chapa’s published Laravel SDK supports payment initialization, verification, and webhook validation; its documented checkout currency is ETB. [Chapa Laravel SDK](https://github.com/Chapa-Et/chapa-laravel), [Chapa payment documentation](https://developer.chapa.co/docs/accept-payments/)
> - Chapa is primary for all new payments; legacy Stripe/PayPal is temporary compatibility only.
> - Subscription renewal is manual per billing period because no Chapa recurring-charge capability has been provided.
</details>

Two final migration details are now clear: all new payments will use Chapa in ETB, and existing payments stay valid until their current period ends, then renew through Chapa. I’m resolving one last safety point: today the app’s default Digital Products currency is USD, so amounts must not be silently relabeled as birr.

Implemented Chapa-first payments across Linket.

- Digital Products now create ETB Chapa hosted checkouts; verified payment creates orders, downloads, receipts, earnings, and payouts.
- New subscriptions and manual renewals use Chapa. Renewals get 7/3/1-day reminders and a 7-day grace period.
- Added signed Chapa webhook/callback verification, exact transaction matching, and idempotent fulfillment.
- Added gateway-neutral `payment_transactions` tracking.
- New ETB-only pricing prevents silent USD conversion; legacy Stripe/PayPal payments remain readable and functional.
- Added Chapa admin settings, checkout UI, polling return screens, API types, and scheduled renewal processing.
- Removed new Stripe/PayPal plan syncing while retaining legacy webhook support.

Verification completed:

- Database migration ran successfully
- PHPUnit: 4 tests passed
- Focused PHPStan: no errors
- API type generation passed
- Production frontend build passed

Before production, set `CHAPA_SECRET_KEY` and `CHAPA_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, enable Chapa in Billing settings, configure Chapa’s webhook URL as `/billing/chapa/webhook`, and run Laravel’s scheduler and queue worker.

Note: the Chapa package uses `dev-main` because its stable release does not support this Laravel 12 app.

> # Production-Ready Digital Product Payments
>
> ## Summary
>
> Complete the buyer payment experience around Chapa: collect buyer details in a Buy-now dialog, reliably send download receipts, make success pages read like order receipts, configure signed webhooks through existing admin settings, and give admins clear failed-payment guidance. Keep phone optional, pass it to Chapa when present, and do not retain it locally.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Replace the direct Buy-now redirect with a compact shadcn dialog:
>   - Required: buyer name and email.
>   - Optional: phone number.
>   - Validate details before creating checkout; send name/email/phone to Chapa where supported.
>   - Persist buyer name and email on the pending order/payment transaction; never persist the optional phone or log it.
>   - Extend the public checkout endpoint to accept the buyer details while retaining its rate limit and public bio-page/product authorization.
>
> - Update payment fulfillment and receipt delivery:
>   - Preserve Linket’s captured buyer email when Chapa does not return one.
>   - Queue one receipt only after verified payment; personalize it with buyer/product/order details and signed download links.
>   - Keep existing idempotency so repeated callbacks/webhooks cannot create duplicate orders, entitlements, or receipts.
>   - Expand the paid success screen into a receipt surface: paid state, product, amount/currency, order reference, buyer email, paid time, and protected download list.
>
> - Finish secure Chapa webhook configuration:
>   - Use the existing Admin Settings Chapa webhook-secret field as the encrypted server-side source, with `CHAPA_WEBHOOK_SECRET` retained as deployment fallback.
>   - Show the exact webhook endpoint and setup checklist in the Chapa settings panel.
>   - Continue rejecting unsigned webhooks; verify the transaction server-to-server before fulfilling.
>   - Keep the callback endpoint as a recovery path, but treat the signed webhook as the primary production notification.
>
> - Improve Admin Payment Activity:
>   - Add a sanitized `failure_reason` to payment attempts and expose it through the admin API/types.
>   - Show a clear status explanation and safe next step in the transaction detail dialog:
>     - Pending: wait for Chapa verification or inspect the reference.
>     - Failed initialization: have the customer begin a fresh checkout.
>     - Failed verification: confirm the Chapa reference, amount, and ETB currency.
>   - Do not add any admin action that manually marks a payment paid.
>
> - Preserve protected-download rules:
>   - Keep seven-day expiry and ten-download cap.
>   - Ensure invalid, expired, or exhausted links return a clear protected-download failure response without exposing the file.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - Checkout rejects missing/invalid buyer name or email; accepts optional phone without storing it.
> - Captured buyer email remains on the paid order when Chapa’s verification payload has no email.
> - Verified payment creates exactly one order fulfillment, entitlement set, creator earnings entry, and queued receipt.
> - Signed webhook succeeds only with the configured secret; invalid signature, unknown reference, amount mismatch, currency mismatch, and duplicate delivery never grant access.
> - Success API/page exposes receipt details and downloads only for the matching paid transaction.
> - Receipt contains the product/order context and signed download URLs.
> - Downloads succeed while valid, fail after seven days, and stop after ten successful uses.
> - Admin payment API/UI shows failure reason and safe retry guidance.
> - Run Laravel tests, PHPStan, generated API types, production frontend build, and one Chapa sandbox webhook delivery.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Buyer name and email are required before checkout; phone is optional and transient.
> - The receipt email is the buyer email entered in Linket, not a value dependent on Chapa.
> - Only Chapa’s signed webhook or server-side transaction verification can mark payment as paid.
> - Admins can investigate and guide customers, but cannot override payment status manually.
</details>

> Plan
>
> # Production Operations and Payment Health
>
> ## Summary
>
> Make payment fulfillment operationally reliable before adding buyer order lookup. Use Redis + Horizon under Supervisor for queued work, cron for Laravel’s scheduler, SMTP through the existing admin mail settings, and a sanitized Chapa webhook-delivery log.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Configure production queue processing:
>   - Set Redis as the production queue/cache backend and run `php artisan horizon` under Supervisor.
>   - Route receipt emails and Chapa subscription reminder notifications onto a dedicated `mail` queue with bounded retries and backoff.
>   - Keep receipt fulfillment idempotent: a retried job must not send another receipt after `receipt_sent_at` is set.
>   - Add a small admin-only “send test email” action that sends to the signed-in administrator and links to the existing outgoing-email log.
>
> - Make subscription automation resilient:
>   - Run `billing:process-chapa-renewals` hourly with overlap protection and single-server locking.
>   - Keep the existing 7/3/1-day reminders, seven-day grace period, cancellation, trial, and expiry rules.
>   - Deploy `php artisan schedule:run` once per minute through Linux cron; use the existing scheduler heartbeat and schedule log as the verification source.
>
> - Add persistent, safe Chapa webhook observability:
>   - Create a webhook-delivery record for recent Chapa attempts: received time, transaction reference when present, signature result, verification/fulfillment outcome, and a safe failure code.
>   - Never store raw webhook bodies, signatures, buyer phone numbers, Chapa secrets, or sensitive verification metadata.
>   - Record invalid signatures, missing/unknown references, verification mismatches, duplicate deliveries, and fulfilled events without changing the existing payment idempotency rules.
>
> - Extend `/admin/transactions` into a Payment health overview:
>   - Add compact health cards for pending/failed Chapa transactions, failed queue jobs, Horizon worker status, scheduler heartbeat, and latest webhook outcome.
>   - Show safe operational guidance and links to Horizon, schedule logs, outgoing-email logs, and the existing transaction detail view.
>   - Show failed-job metadata limited to queue, job class, failure time, and a sanitized error summary; do not expose job payloads or add manual “mark paid” controls.
>   - Add an admin-only payment-health API endpoint and generated client types.
>
> - Add Linux deployment assets and checks:
>   - Provide Supervisor configuration for Horizon with graceful restart settings.
>   - Provide cron configuration for `schedule:run`, plus deployment steps for cache/config refresh and `php artisan horizon:terminate`.
>   - Document SMTP sender configuration in Admin Settings, Redis environment variables, and health checks for mail, Horizon, scheduler, and Chapa webhooks.
>   - Do not configure or test the Chapa signing secret in this milestone; retain the existing encrypted settings field and deployment fallback.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - Receipt and reminder jobs use the `mail` queue, retry safely, and remain idempotent.
> - A configured mailer can send the admin test email; delivery appears in the outgoing-email log.
> - Renewal processing sends each 7/3/1-day reminder once, applies grace status, and expires access after seven days.
> - Webhook delivery records are created for accepted, rejected, duplicate, unknown-reference, and verification-failure cases without persisting secrets or payloads.
> - Payment-health API and UI correctly report worker, scheduler, payment, failed-job, and webhook state with admin-only authorization.
> - Run Laravel tests, PHPStan, generated API types, and a production frontend build.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - This milestone is operations only; buyer email order lookup and receipt/download resend follow next.
> - Production uses Redis with Horizon under Linux Supervisor and one cron entry for Laravel’s scheduler.
> - SMTP remains the default mail transport, configured through the existing Admin Settings with a verified sender address.
> - Chapa signed-webhook delivery will be tested later after the signing secret is available.
</details>

> Plan
>
> # Digital Products Finance & Withdrawal System
>
> ## Summary
>
> Strengthen Linket’s Digital Products finance foundation with an immutable creator-earnings ledger, a staged manual payout workflow, admin-managed withdrawal methods, and refund-safe transaction records. Use the useful staged-withdrawal ideas from `diget`, but retain Linket’s verified Chapa payments and avoid mutable user-balance accounting.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Replace computed-only creator balances with an append-only Digital Products earnings ledger.
>   - Verified Chapa product payments create one held creator-earning entry using the existing order fee/earning snapshots.
>   - Earnings become available after the default seven-day hold.
>   - Payout reservations, rejected/cancelled payout releases, refunds, and admin adjustments become auditable ledger entries.
>   - Available balance always reflects held funds, available earnings, active payout reservations, paid withdrawals, and refunds—including negative balance carry-forward after a seller has already been paid.
>
> - Expand payout requests into a safe state machine:
>   - `requested` → `processing` → `paid`
>   - `requested`/`processing` → `rejected` or `cancelled`
>   - A creator can cancel only an unprocessed request; cancellation or rejection releases reserved funds.
>   - Admins must supply a transfer reference when marking a payout paid, plus optional internal notes.
>   - Every transition records actor, timestamp, reason/note, and creates an auditable activity entry.
>   - Creator and admin notifications are queued after request, approval, rejection, payment, cancellation, and refund-impact events.
>
> - Add admin-managed withdrawal methods.
>   - Admins create, enable/disable, order, and configure methods such as Bank Transfer, Telebirr, PayPal, and Other.
>   - Each method has a label, instructions, minimum withdrawal amount, optional maximum, and required destination guidance.
>   - Creators choose an enabled method and save one active encrypted payout destination per workspace.
>   - Payout requests snapshot the selected method, masked destination, and encrypted destination data so later edits do not alter historic requests.
>   - Only authorized payout-review admins can reveal a destination; each reveal is audit-logged.
>
> - Upgrade creator Sales & Payouts.
>   - Show Held, Available, Reserved, Paid out, and Lifetime earnings with compact sales and payout history.
>   - Clearly show the expected availability date for held earnings.
>   - Let creators manage their withdrawal method, request a valid amount, view status history, and cancel eligible requests.
>   - Keep Digital Products sales separate from subscription-plan billing.
>
> - Upgrade admin Payments and Payouts.
>   - `/admin/transactions` remains the Chapa payment activity source: payment status, buyer, product/subscription target, failure reason, verified reference, and refund history.
>   - `/admin/digital-products/payouts` becomes the payout operations queue with filters for state, creator, method, date, and amount.
>   - Payout detail shows creator, earnings availability, method snapshot, masked/revealable destination, transition history, transfer reference, and notes.
>   - Add manual refund recording for paid Digital Product transactions: admin completes the Chapa refund outside Linket, then records a full or partial refund amount and reason in Linket.
>   - A recorded refund is idempotent, cannot exceed the paid amount, reverses the proportional creator earning and platform fee snapshot, and revokes download access only when the order is fully refunded.
>
> - Keep payment boundaries secure.
>   - Only verified Chapa transactions can credit creator earnings.
>   - Payouts never use Chapa transfers or Stripe Connect in this milestone; all payouts remain manual.
>   - Store account destinations encrypted; never expose them in creator list APIs, logs, webhook metadata, or generated admin table data.
>   - Preserve existing Chapa webhook idempotency, protected downloads, receipt flow, and payment-health monitoring.
>
> ## API and Data Interfaces
>
> - Add ledger, payout-activity, payout-method configuration, refund, and destination-reveal records/resources.
> - Creator APIs:
>   - finance summary and earnings history;
>   - enabled withdrawal methods;
>   - active withdrawal destination;
>   - payout request, cancellation, and history.
> - Admin APIs:
>   - withdrawal-method CRUD;
>   - payout queue/detail and state transitions;
>   - audited payout-destination reveal;
>   - Digital Product transaction refund recording and refund history.
> - Keep current payout-request routes as compatibility aliases while the creator/admin frontend moves to the richer finance APIs.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - Verified Digital Product payment creates exactly one held ledger credit with the correct fee and creator-earning snapshots.
> - Seven-day hold, early admin release, payout reservation, rejection, cancellation, paid payout, and negative refund carry-forward calculate balances correctly.
> - Only enabled methods can be selected; destinations are encrypted, masked by default, and reveal actions require admin authorization and create an audit record.
> - Invalid payout amounts, duplicate active requests, insufficient available balance, invalid state transitions, and missing payment references are rejected.
> - Refunds are idempotent, cannot exceed the original payment, correctly reverse earnings, and only revoke entitlements after a full refund.
> - Creator workspace isolation, admin-only finance operations, ledger immutability, queued notifications, generated API types, Laravel tests, PHPStan, and production frontend build all pass.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Digital Product earnings use a default seven-day hold before withdrawal eligibility.
> - Admins may release a specific held earning early only with an auditable reason.
> - Refunds are performed manually in Chapa and recorded in Linket; Linket does not initiate Chapa refunds automatically.
> - One creator has one active encrypted withdrawal destination per workspace, selected from admin-managed withdrawal methods.
</details>

> # Buyer Order Lookup & Receipt Recovery
>
> ## Summary
>
> Replace the current reference-based public order lookup with a secure, email-only recovery flow. Buyers receive a one-time recovery link, view only their paid Digital Product purchases, resend receipts, and access downloads that are still valid. Admins get a privacy-safe delivery history.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Add `/find-my-purchase` with an email form and generic confirmation message to prevent account enumeration.
>   - Rate limit requests by normalized-email hash and IP address.
>   - Queue a recovery email only when paid orders exist; never reveal whether an email has purchases.
>   - Create recovery records with a hashed opaque token, encrypted email, expiry, redeemed time, and delivery status.
>
> - Use a one-time email link valid for 30 minutes.
>   - Redeeming it creates a 30-minute secure, HttpOnly recovery session and redirects to `/find-my-purchase/orders`.
>   - The private purchase page shows only paid orders for that email, with product, order reference, payment date, amount, receipt status, and eligible downloads.
>   - Generate download URLs only inside the authenticated recovery session; preserve the existing seven-day expiry, revocation, and ten-download cap.
>
> - Replace the unsafe public lookup response.
>   - Remove direct order/download access from the existing email-plus-reference endpoint.
>   - Add recovery request, token redemption, private orders, download-link, and receipt-resend APIs.
>   - Keep resend actions rate-limited per order and recovery session; receipts use the original entitlement limits and never extend access.
>
> - Reuse the existing receipt job with recovery-safe behavior.
>   - Send one receipt per explicit resend request, retaining idempotent fulfillment and normal outgoing-mail logging.
>   - Include product/order context and only currently valid signed download links.
>   - Do not persist buyer phone numbers or expose entitlement URLs in admin APIs.
>
> - Add an admin-only Digital Product delivery-history view.
>   - Show masked buyer email, order reference, product, event type, queued/sent/failed status, timestamp, and safe failure summary.
>   - Track recovery requests, recovery-email delivery, receipt resend requests, receipt delivery, and failures.
>   - Exclude download URLs, payout destinations, payout details, raw mail content, tokens, and sensitive job payloads.
>
> ## Tests
>
> - Email-only recovery always returns the same public response for known, unknown, unpaid, and malformed-order cases.
> - Rate limits apply by email hash and IP; tokens are hashed, expire after 30 minutes, and cannot be redeemed twice.
> - A recovery session exposes only that buyer’s paid orders and only currently valid downloads.
> - Expired, revoked, exhausted, or fully refunded entitlements remain inaccessible.
> - Receipt resend is rate-limited, uses the original entitlement window/count, and does not duplicate fulfillment.
> - Admin delivery history is admin-only and masks email while excluding download and payout data.
> - Run Laravel tests, generated API types, PHPStan, and the production frontend build.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Recovery links are one-time and create a 30-minute browser session.
> - Admin delivery history shows masked email addresses.
> - Resending a receipt never refreshes the seven-day expiry or ten-download limit.
</details>

> title: Skills
> description: Give your AI assistant deep knowledge of shadcn/ui components, patterns, and best practices.
> ---
>
> Skills give AI assistants like Claude Code project-aware context about shadcn/ui. When installed, your AI assistant knows how to find, install, compose, and customize components using the correct APIs and patterns for your project.
>
> For example, you can ask your AI assistant to:
>
> - *"Add a login form with email and password fields."*
> - *"Create a settings page with a form for updating profile information."*
> - *"Build a dashboard with a sidebar, stats cards, and a data table."*
> - *"Switch to --preset [CODE]"*
> - *"Can you add a hero from @tailark?"*
>
> The skill reads your project's `components.json` and provides the assistant with your framework, aliases, installed components, icon library, and base library so it can generate correct code on the first try.
>
> ---
>
> ## Install
>
> ```bash
> npx skills add shadcn/ui
> ```
>
> This installs the shadcn skill into your project. Once installed, your AI assistant automatically loads it when working with shadcn/ui components.
>
> Learn more about skills at [skills.sh](https://skills.sh).
>
> ---
>
> ## What's Included
>
> The skill provides your AI assistant with the following knowledge:
>
> ### Project Context
>
> On every interaction, the skill runs `shadcn info --json` to get your project's configuration: framework, Tailwind version, aliases, base library (`base`, `radix`, or `aria`), icon library, installed components, and resolved file paths.
>
> ### CLI Commands
>
> Full reference for all CLI commands: `init`, `add`, `search`, `view`, `docs`, `diff`, `info`, and `build`. Includes flags, dry-run mode, smart merge workflows, presets, and templates.
>
> ### Theming and Customization
>
> How CSS variables, OKLCH colors, dark mode, custom colors, border radius, and component variants work. Includes guidance for both Tailwind v3 and v4.
>
> ### Registry Authoring
>
> How to build and publish custom component registries: `registry.json` format, item types, file objects, dependencies, CSS variables, building, hosting, and user configuration.
>
> ### MCP Server
>
> Setup and tools for the shadcn MCP server, which lets AI assistants search, browse, and install components from registries.
>
> ---
>
> ## How It Works
>
> 1. **Project detection** — The skill activates when it finds a `components.json` file in your project.
> 2. **Context injection** — It runs `shadcn info --json` to read your project configuration and injects the result into the assistant's context.
> 3. **Pattern enforcement** — The assistant follows shadcn/ui composition rules: using `FieldGroup` for forms, `ToggleGroup` for option sets, semantic colors, and correct base-specific APIs.
> 4. **Component discovery** — The assistant uses `shadcn docs`, `shadcn search`, or MCP tools to find components and their documentation before generating code.
>
> ## Learn More
>
> - [CLI](/docs/cli) — Full CLI command reference
> - [MCP Server](/docs/mcp) — Connect the MCP server for registry access
> - [Theming](/docs/theming) — CSS variables and customization
> - [Registry](/docs/registry) — Building and publishing custom registries
> - [skills.sh](https://skills.sh) — Learn more about AI skills
>

> Plan

> # Fixed Creator Profile & Store Builder
>
> ## Summary
>
> Replace the open-ended widget experience with a structured creator-profile builder. New pages use one responsive two-column layout: creator profile card on the left and creator work plus Digital Products on the right. Existing pages remain functional and can be upgraded without deleting their original content.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - Add `builder_mode` and validated `profile_config` data to biolinks.
>   - New pages default to `creator_profile`; existing pages remain `legacy`.
>   - Store display name, headline, bio, avatar, cover, availability, skills, social links, follow URL, and contact URL per page.
>   - Reuse the existing image uploader for avatar and cover images.
>   - Verification status and public item statistics remain server-controlled.
>
> - Rebuild `/dashboard/biolinks/{id}` for creator-profile pages.
>   - Replace “Add link” and “Add widget” with fixed editor sections: Profile, Social links, Actions, Work, Appearance, and Insights.
>   - Use compact shadcn fields and accordions with `Trans`, Lucide icons, existing design tokens, and a synchronized preview.
>   - Keep one fixed layout with desktop/mobile preview controls; remove layout selection.
>   - Follow uses a selected social URL, Message uses an email/contact URL, and Tip remains hidden until native tipping exists.
>
> - Add a curated Work area.
>   - Allow at most six creator-managed image, text, or link showcase items.
>   - Reuse existing image, text, and link records/renderers behind the structured editor.
>   - Remove the general widget selector and prevent unsupported widgets from being added to creator-profile pages through the API.
>   - Digital Products remains automatically managed from product-to-bio-page assignments and does not count against the six-item limit.
>
> - Build the public creator page.
>   - Desktop: compact profile card in a roughly 360px left column; Work and Digital Products in the flexible right column.
>   - Mobile: profile, Work, and Digital Products stack naturally without a nested page container.
>   - Profile card includes cover, overlapping avatar, availability badge, name, verified indicator when applicable, headline, configured actions, bio, up to eight skills, social icons, and published item count.
>   - Product cards use a responsive one-, two-, or three-column grid and retain canonical product-detail links.
>   - Hide public sales and review statistics until creator privacy controls and a real review system exist.
>   - Preserve page background, font, accent color, branding rules, custom domains, analytics, and approved-product visibility.
>
> - Add guided legacy conversion.
>   - Existing public pages and their current editor continue working until the creator chooses “Upgrade to Creator Profile.”
>   - Conversion maps the first avatar image, first profile text, social widget, existing links, compatible image/text content, and managed Shop widget.
>   - Unsupported embeds remain stored but are not shown after conversion; the confirmation dialog lists them before conversion.
>   - Conversion is idempotent and never deletes legacy widget records.
>
> ## APIs and Safeguards
>
> - Extend the biolink resource with `builder_mode`, validated creator-profile data, server-derived item count, and actual verification status.
> - Add authenticated profile update and legacy-conversion endpoints under the existing versioned biolink API.
> - Restrict creator-profile content mutations to the approved work types and six-item quota; managed Shop sections are updated only by Digital Product visibility logic.
> - Enforce workspace ownership, URL validation, profile length limits, maximum eight skills, upload permissions, and existing biolink policies.
> - Regenerate frontend API types after the backend contract is complete.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - New pages receive creator-profile mode and sensible defaults from the signed-in creator.
> - Existing legacy pages render unchanged until explicitly converted.
> - Conversion maps compatible content, preserves unsupported records, and is safe when repeated.
> - Unauthorized workspace users cannot read or modify creator-profile settings or uploads.
> - Creator-profile pages reject unsupported widgets and more than six work items.
> - Follow, Message, social links, availability, verification, and public item count render from the correct trusted sources.
> - Digital Products show only approved products assigned to that page and remain outside the work-item quota.
> - Public desktop and mobile layouts have no overflow, duplicated Shop headings, nested page shell, or empty placeholder statistics.
> - Run focused Laravel PHPUnit tests, generated API types, TypeScript checks, and the production frontend build.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Guided opt-in conversion is used instead of automatically changing existing pages.
> - The fixed Work area supports image, text, and link items only.
> - Follow and Message are real configured links; Tip is hidden.
> - Only the published item count is public in this milestone; sales and reviews are deferred.
